Suppose the wood path ends up with a different deadline, event string, recipe route or action dispatch. Both new default-goal tests still pass, and four of my five mutants also pass every one of the 34 tests in the file. So S1's only bridge-level guard of wood invariance would not catch the regression, and the frozen 87673b8 checkpoint would then run on changed helpers in every stone run.

The stand-in has recipesFor/recipesAll returning [] (line 850) and pathfinder.goto always rejecting (line 843). As a result no craft (actions 2, 3, 4, 7), PLACE_TABLE, APPROACH_TABLE, digBlock (where S1 added the pickaxe_digs counter), canopy descent, leaf escape, pickup or successful navigation ever runs. suggested_fix: Extend the stand-in so the same request script drives every wood action against both bridges and compares the answers, with the measured duration removed. Give it a reachable log whose dig succeeds (bot.dig resolving and setting the block to air), a pickup, real recipesFor/recipesAll from prismarine-recipe with a bot.craft that changes the inventory, a placeable table, and a goto that resolves for near goals. Then run [CHOP, CRAFT_PLANKS, CRAFT_STICKS, CRAFT_TABLE, PLACE_TABLE, APPROACH_TABLE, CRAFT_PICKAXE]. Also record each bot.dig/craft/goto call with its goal and timeout, and compare those call logs. title: The equivalence check silently skips without git history, so checks() reports green with no wood comparison
failure_scenario: Tests run from an exported tree, a CI or teammate clone made with --depth that lacks 409560e, or any folder outside a git checkout. There git show fails, the test calls t.skip, and node --test exits 0 with 'skipped 1'. infrastructure checks() and the build report then read as all-pass even though the default-goal invariance was never compared.
evidence: Line 960: if (shown.status !== 0) { t.skip(...); return }. I copied resource-bridge.js, stone-helpers.js and resource-bridge.test.js to scratchpad/review/wood-invariance/nogit and ran node --test --test-name-pattern='exactly as the 409560e'. Output: 'pass 0, fail 0, skipped 1'.
suggested_fix: Commit the 409560e bridge as a fixture file (for example minecraft_bridge/fixtures/resource-bridge-409560e.js, with its SHA-256 asserted in the test) instead of reading git history. Alternatively, make a missing baseline a failure unless an explicit environment variable allows the skip.

verification.reasoning:
I reproduced the mechanism, so this is CONFIRMED. The default-goal equivalence test (minecraft_bridge/resource-bridge.test.js:958-990) gets its baseline only from `git show 409560e:minecraft_bridge/resource-bridge.js` at line 959. When that command fails, line 960 calls t.skip and returns. Node counts a skip as a pass: `node --test` exits 0, and infrastructure/__main__.py checks() (lines 89-108) only looks at return codes, so it still prints "All available checks passed". In the real worktree the test does run and pass. git is on PATH there, because local_environment() only adds to PATH, and the baseline is a 60,711-byte blob (29c792f8...), well below spawnSync's maxBuffer. So nothing breaks in the user's own environment today.

The gap is more than an exported-tree corner case, though. 409560e is not an ancestor of main or origin/main; only codex/pc-canopy-descent (local and origin) and codex/stone-tools contain it. If this work is squash-merged or rebased onto main and the codex branch is deleted, or a teammate clones only main with --single-branch, the baseline is missing. The one bridge-level wood-invariance check would then quietly stop running, which is exactly when later edits to the wood path most need it.

Why it stays low:
- "Silently" is an overstatement. Node prints a skip line with the reason, and the builders disclosed the skip in build_reports.txt (lines 317 and 348).
- The design does not require a git-based comparison. Section 4.12 item 1 only requires that the default goal leave wood runs unchanged.
- It has no runtime effect. The overnight wood run goes from the main checkout, which does not contain this change.
- The skip matches an existing project pattern: the minecraft-data Python cross-check also skips without NODE_PATH.

title: Under the default goal every wood observation still changes: inventory_counts gains stone_materials and stone_pickaxes, and the comment says it is unchanged
failure_scenario: A wood run with the default goal and no survey writes start.json, transitions.jsonl and outcome.json final observations whose inventory_counts has 7 keys instead of the 5 at 409560e. Every wood observation (and CHOP's collected() poll) also now depends on stone-helpers.js: a throw in stoneInventoryCounts, or a load error in that module from a later S3 edit, invalidates every wood episode at its first observation. Before S1 the wood bridge had no stone dependency. Behaviour does not change: Python reads only the 5 wood counts, and the fresh-start any() check still passes. The design asks for these counts in inventoryCounts (4.12 item 2) and docs/resource_training.md discloses them. However, the bridge comment at lines 620-623 says that without the goal or the survey 'the wood stage's observations and their cost are unchanged', which is not true.
evidence: Line 425: return { ...counts, ...stoneHelpers().stoneInventoryCounts(inventory) }. observe() puts it on every observation as inventory_counts: counts (line 862). The equivalence test has to strip the two keys before comparing with 409560e (lines 973-977). Load cost measured with scratchpad/review/wood-invariance/loadtime.js and loadtime2.js: stone-helpers takes about 70 ms the first time, of which about 50 ms is the 1.21.4 registry that createBot would load anyway, so the net cost is about 25 ms before createBot. The added work per observation is negligible.
suggested_fix: For exact wood invariance, add the two stone counts only when stoneFields is true (inventoryCounts(inv, { stone: stoneFields })), so that a default-goal observation is byte-identical to 409560e. Otherwise keep the design's behaviour but correct the comment at lines 620-623 to say that inventory_counts always carries the two stone counts.

verification.reasoning:
Only one part of the claim holds up: the comment at resource-bridge.js:620-623 is inaccurate. The wood-invariance concern itself is refuted.

1. The two extra keys are real, and the design asks for them. Under the default goal, inventory_counts now has 7 keys. Design 3.6, first bullet, lists "inventory_counts.stone_materials and stone_pickaxes, in inventoryCounts". Design 4.12 item 2 says "inventoryCounts: add the new counts". docs/resource_training.md states that every observation's inventory_counts has both counts and that the wood state ignores them. So the reviewer's first fix option (add the counts only when stoneFields is true) goes against the design and the docs, and should not be made.

2. Wood behaviour does not change.
   - Python reads only the five wood fields: state_from_observation and the potential use INVENTORY_FIELDS, and resource_report's _counts uses named keys.
   - The fresh-start any() check at resource_session.py:366 cannot change outcome. The bridge's initialize() already throws unless the whole inventory is empty (line 916), so the stone counts are always 0 there.
   - The 409560e side-by-side test strips the two keys, asserts they are [0, 0], and requires everything else to match.

3. The new dependency on stone-helpers.js is overstated.
   - stoneInventoryCounts cannot throw where the wood loop would not. It runs the same integer check after the wood loop, which runs first over the same entries.
   - main() loads stone-helpers unconditionally at line 597, before createBot. A load error from a later edit would therefore stop the bridge at launch under every goal, not mid-episode at the first observation. Removing the counts from inventoryCounts would not change this.
   - The design puts the module there (4.12 item 4), and resource_session.py:320-325 hashes stone-helpers.js, so a change to it stops the next episode like any other source change.

4. The overnight wood run is not affected. The main checkout is at 409560e, and later stone runs use --goal stone_pickaxe, where the stone fields are present anyway.

What remains is the comment. It cites "The stone fields (section 3.6)" and concludes that without the goal or the survey "the wood stage's observations and their cost are unchanged". Section 3.6 includes the inventory counts, and those are always present, so observations do change by two zero-valued keys. The cost clause is roughly true: about 25 ms of load at startup and a trivial loop per observation. This is a comment-accuracy issue only, so low severity.

title: The wood policy layout is chosen by object identity, so a copied or pickled wood agent saves a 'stage' key and is no longer byte-identical
failure_scenario: A future caller deep-copies a wood ResourceAgent, for example to snapshot a checkpoint or to evaluate a copy, or passes it through pickle or multiprocessing, and then calls save(). The copy's stage is a new StageSpec object, so 'self.stage is WOOD_STAGE' is False and the file gains "stage": "wood" after format_version. The byte-identity guarantee, which the golden SHA-256 tests pin only for agents built directly, breaks silently. The file still loads in the new code and in 409560e. No current caller in minecraft_rl, infrastructure or scripts copies or pickles agents, so this is latent.
evidence: scratchpad/review/wood-invariance/copy_check.py output: 'deepcopy stage is WOOD_STAGE: False | saved keys start: [format_version, stage, environment]'; 'pickle ... False | [format_version, stage, environment]'; 'copy ... True | [format_version, environment, algorithm]'. Line 365: stage = {} if self.stage is WOOD_STAGE else {"stage": self.stage.name}.
suggested_fix: Decide by name: stage = {} if self.stage.name == WOOD_STAGE.name else {"stage": self.stage.name}. Since load treats a missing key as wood, the two are equivalent. Alternatively, give StageSpec __deepcopy__/__reduce__ methods that return the module-level singleton.

verification.reasoning:
I could not refute this. I reproduced it against the worktree's own module. Line 365 of minecraft_rl/resources.py picks the layout with `self.stage is WOOD_STAGE`. StageSpec is `@dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False)` and defines no __deepcopy__ or __reduce__, so copy.deepcopy and pickle both build a new StageSpec object. Because eq=False, `==` is also identity, so it fails the same way. A wood agent that has been deep-copied or pickled therefore saves with "stage": "wood" right after format_version, and its text no longer matches the 409560e layout. The code's own comment ("Wood policies keep their original layout") and the golden SHA-256 tests in tests/test_resources.py (GOLDEN_POLICY_SHA256, lines 257-329) treat that layout as a guarantee, and those tests only cover agents built directly. A shallow copy.copy keeps the reference, so it is unaffected.

The impact is latent and small. No caller in minecraft_rl, infrastructure or scripts deep-copies or pickles a ResourceAgent. The only save calls are experiments.py:62, __main__.py:69 and resource_session.py:121, and each saves an agent built or loaded directly. infrastructure/parallel_runs.py's save() writes its own run state, not agents. A loaded agent gets stage=WOOD_STAGE through the default argument, so it still saves byte-identically.

Nothing in how the wood stage behaves depends on identity: act, update, allowed and validate go through the copied spec's attributes, and actions_for keeps pointing to the same module function. A file with "stage": "wood" still loads in the new code, and in the 409560e code, which ignores the extra key (I checked both). The design (section 4 item 5, S1 in section 9) only requires that resource_v1 checkpoints stay loadable, which holds either way. Byte-identity of saved files is the builders' own stricter promise, and this break only touches a hash nobody computes today.

The overnight wood run uses the main checkout, and the frozen wood checkpoint is only loaded, never re-saved, so neither is affected. Severity stays low: it is a real hole in a stated guarantee, but no current code path can reach it.
verification.evidence:
Scratch script C:\Users\ethan\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-ethan-PycharmProjects-RL-Minecraft-project\e8caeeaf-7c0d-42d8-a0e0-47974dda527c\scratchpad\review\refute-wood-identity\check.py, run with the worktree's minecraft_rl/resources.py (an unmasked wood agent after one update):

The line itself (resources.py:365): `stage = {} if self.stage is WOOD_STAGE else {"stage": self.stage.name}`. StageSpec is declared `@dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False)` (line 236) with no copy or pickle hooks. verification.fix_notes:
Decide by name at line 365: `stage = {} if self.stage.name == WOOD_STAGE.name else {"stage": self.stage.name}`. This matches load, which reads a missing key as "wood" (line 386), so save and load then use the same rule. It is safe: a spec named "wood" whose actions, fields or caps differ is still refused by load's existing checks of actions, state_fields, state_caps and conditions.

Do not switch to `==`: with eq=False it is identity too.

The alternative is to give StageSpec `__reduce__` and `__deepcopy__` methods that return the module-level singleton. That needs a name-to-spec registry across resources.py and stone.py, so it is more invasive for no extra benefit here.

Add a regression test next to the golden SHA tests: save `copy.deepcopy(agent)` and `pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(agent))` for each golden wood agent, and assert the text matches GOLDEN_POLICY_SHA256 and has no "stage" key. Also assert that a stone agent, copied the same way, still saves "stage": "stone".

None of this blocks the overnight wood run or any current caller. It can be fixed with the other S1 review findings.

title: The wood agent constructor now accepts None for action_mask or state_version and has a different error text
failure_scenario: At 409560e, ResourceAgent(action_mask=None) or ResourceAgent(state_version=None) raised ValueError 'Unsupported condition: ...'. Now either None silently becomes the masked/resource_v1 condition. A caller that forwards an unset condition, for example a future scheduler or S3 coordinator passing None for 'not given', would silently train or evaluate under the masked condition instead of failing. Every other unsupported pair now says 'Unsupported wood condition: ...' instead of 'Unsupported condition: ...'. No current caller passes None, and nothing matches on the old text.
evidence: scratchpad/review/wood-invariance/diff_agent.py (old resources.py from git show 409560e loaded beside the new one): "CTOR DIFF {'action_mask': None} old: ValueError Unsupported condition: action_mask=None, state_version='resource_v1' new: ok masked"; the same for state_version=None; for action_mask='bogus' the old message is 'Unsupported condition: ...' and the new one is 'Unsupported wood condition: ...'.
suggested_fix: Use a private sentinel (or keep the old MASKED/POLICY_ENVIRONMENT defaults when stage is WOOD_STAGE) so that an explicit None is still refused. Keep the old message text for the wood stage, or accept the new text and document it.

verification.reasoning:
The facts in the claim are right, but they are not a defect, and the wood stage's behaviour is not affected.

1. The change is deliberate and documented. Each stage now needs its own defaults: a stone-stage agent cannot default to MASKED/resource_v1. So the signature became `action_mask: str | None = None, state_version: str | None = None`, and the docstring says they "default to the stage's default condition". Passing None means "not given", and that now gets the default. This is what the reviewer's imagined future caller would want, not a silent wrong condition.

2. The project already treats an unset condition this way. At 409560e, resource_session.py does `CONDITIONS[condition or "masked"]`, and the CLI's `--condition` defaults to None, which means masked. The constructor now follows the same rule.

3. No caller passes None. resource_session.py:266-268, train_simulator (resources.py:576) and scripts/resource_budget_study.py:64 all take the pair from CONDITIONS[...]. On the load path, `ResourceAgent.load` checks `(payload.get("action_mask"), version) in stage.conditions.values()` before it calls the constructor. A policy file with `action_mask: null` is therefore still refused, with the same message as before.

4. The design does not require refusing None. docs/stone_tools_design.md section 11 item 5 asks only that `ResourceAgent` be generalized over a stage specification, with resource_v1 checkpoints still loadable. Wood invariance is about run behaviour (action 6, safeMovements, the CHOP action, the default goal), not about which values the Python constructor accepts.

5. The new error text is not matched anywhere (git grep at 409560e and at HEAD finds no test, script or doc that does). The module-level `condition_name` still raises the old "Unsupported condition: ..." text. Only the constructor's message gained the stage name, and that helps once two stages exist.

6. The frozen checkpoint is unaffected. The old and new code load it into the same condition (unmasked) and the same Q table, and it saves back byte for byte the same.

title: time_of_day sits behind the wooden-pickaxe latch, so stage-1 observations and stage-1 failures never record it
failure_scenario: Design 4.10 says the bridge records time_of_day in every observation and flags episodes that pass tick 12000, and 8.3 reports game time at the end. A stage-1 episode that runs its 60 decisions into the night carries no time at all, so it cannot be flagged.
evidence: observeStone returns the all-null fields before the latch (resource-bridge.js:885-886); time_of_day is filled only inside the latched branch (:893).

verification.reasoning:
The code shows the defect plainly, and I reproduced it offline. In observeStone (resource-bridge.js:881-904) the fields object starts with time_of_day: null. The latch `stoneStarted = stoneStarted || counts.pickaxes > 0` then returns that object unchanged until a wooden pickaxe has been in the inventory (:885-886). time_of_day is read from bot.time.timeOfDay only inside the latched branch (:893). So under --goal stone_pickaxe, every stage-1 observation carries time_of_day null, and so does the last observation of a stage-1 failure.

The design asks for more than this. Section 4.10 says "The bridge records time_of_day in every observation, and episodes that pass tick 12000 are flagged". Section 8.3 lists "game time at the end" among the reported outcomes, and stage-1 failures are episodes too: they count in C1 and in "stage-1 success per arm". The only gating rule in the design, section 3.6 ("The stone scans run only once a wooden pickaxe is in the inventory, so the wood stage's observation cost stays as it was"), covers the scans. Reading bot.time.timeOfDay is not a scan and reads no blocks, so nothing in the design requires latching it. The builder raised exactly this as an open question in build_reports.txt: "I followed the task and gated it with the other stone fields, so stage-1 observations, including stage-1 failures, carry no time_of_day."

Severity stays low:
- It is a gap in a diagnostic. It does not affect safety or learning: no state encoder reads time_of_day (stone.py and resources.py never reference it, and test_resource_session shows the wood state ignores the stone fields).
- Every episode that reaches stage 2 gets a time at the hand-off and afterwards. Only stage-1 failures lose it, and the design estimates 0–2 of those per arm.
- The default goal is untouched: stoneFields is false there, so the field is absent. The overnight wood run and the frozen checkpoint are not affected, and neither would be by the fix.

title: stone_targets lists only reach candidates, so the target behind stone_visible=1 is recorded nowhere outside the survey
failure_scenario: Design 3.6 defines stone_targets as 'the up to 3 nearest seen targets'. The bridge fills it from the reach list, so whenever stone_visible=1 and nearby_stone=0 (the case where SEARCH_STONE walks), stone_targets is []. The fan targets appear only in diagnostic_only.fan.nearest, which exists only with --stone-survey. In the live experiment no observation says which target SEARCH_STONE was steering to, so stone_path_blocked failures cannot be traced from the observations.
evidence: resource-bridge.js:519 `stone_targets: reach.slice(0, 3).map(...)`; the fan targets appear only at :577 inside stoneSurveyRecord.
suggested_fix: Also record the fan's next target, the one memory.peek returns, as stone_search_target, or the 3 nearest fan targets, in every stone-stage observation. Or document the deviation from 3.6.

verification.reasoning: The code does what the reviewer says, and the design asks for something else. Design 3.6 defines `stone_targets` as "the up to 3 nearest seen targets". The design uses "seen" and "targets" for discovery: 4.2 is headed "Discovery (`stone_visible`, the targets of `SEARCH_STONE`)" and lists ray-fan "Targets", while the reach list is described as "candidates" (3.2, 4.5). The wood observation follows the same pattern: `nearby_visible_logs` is `visibleLogs().slice(0, 3)`, the 3 nearest visible logs at search range, not the logs in reach. In `stoneScan` (resource-bridge.js:519), `stone_targets` is `reach.slice(0, 3)`, so it holds MINE_STONE's in-reach candidates only. When `stone_visible=1` and `nearby_stone=0` (the case where SEARCH_STONE walks), it is `[]` even though `fan.targets` is not empty. The fan targets appear only in `diagnostic_only.fan.nearest` (:577), and only when `--stone-survey` is on and `stageStartY` is set. Under `--goal stone_pickaxe` without the survey, no observation records them. The builder's report says it followed its task text ("stone_targets come from the reach list, as the task says"), not the spec. No Python code reads `stone_targets` (it is recorded only, and no state encoder uses it), so state, actions, reward, digging safety and the wood stage are unaffected. Under the default goal the stone fields are absent and no scan runs. The S2 survey loses nothing either, because `diagnostic_only.fan.nearest` has the fan targets. What is lost is traceability in S3 and later stone runs without the survey: a `stone_path_blocked` result cannot be tied to the block SEARCH_STONE was steering to. title: Stage is checked by object identity, so a copied or unpickled agent changes the wood file layout and a copied stone agent cannot be evaluated
failure_scenario: Any agent passed through copy.deepcopy or pickle (for example the S5 budget study sending agents to worker processes for its 3,240 cells, or a test that snapshots an agent) gets a new StageSpec object. A copied wood agent then saves with a "stage": "wood" key, so the file is no longer byte-identical to the 409560e format and its digest changes. A copied stone agent is refused by evaluate_stone_policy (stone.py:495, `agent.stage is not STONE_STAGE`). No current caller copies or pickles agents (grep found no deepcopy, pickle or multiprocessing in minecraft_rl, infrastructure or scripts), so the problem is latent today.
evidence: resources.py:365 `stage = {} if self.stage is WOOD_STAGE else {"stage": self.stage.name}`; stone.py:495 `agent.stage is not STONE_STAGE`. StageSpec is `@dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False)`, so equality is identity. Scratch script review/python-stone/identity.py printed: `deepcopy wood clone stage is WOOD_STAGE: False | saved keys start: ['format_version', 'stage', 'environment']`, the same for pickle, and `deepcopy stone clone refused: A stone evaluation needs a stone-stage ResourceAgent`, the same for pickle.
suggested_fix: Compare stages by name (`self.stage.name == WOOD_STAGE.name`; `agent.stage.name == STONE_STAGE.name` together with the actions check), or give StageSpec a `__reduce__`/`__deepcopy__` that returns the registered singleton by name. Add a test that saves a deep-copied and an unpickled wood agent and checks byte identity.

verification.reasoning:
The mechanism is real and I reproduced it. StageSpec is `@dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False)` and has no `__reduce__` or `__deepcopy__`, so copy.deepcopy and pickle each build a new StageSpec instance. Two checks then fail because they test identity:
- resources.py:365, `stage = {} if self.stage is WOOD_STAGE else {"stage": self.stage.name}`, gives a cloned wood agent the extra `"stage": "wood"` key.
- stone.py:495, `agent.stage is not STONE_STAGE`, refuses a cloned stone agent.

At 409560e, save() had no stage concept, so a deep-copied wood agent wrote the legacy layout. In principle this is a small regression against that format.

It is latent today, and the design does not ask for copying or pickling:
- Every construction and load site passes the module singletons: resources.py:576 builds wood agents with the default stage, stone.py:446 uses `stage=STONE_STAGE`, and resource_session.py:255/267 and resource_budget_study.py:64 use defaults.
- The repo has no deepcopy, pickle, multiprocessing or concurrent.futures on agents. The deepcopy calls in tests copy payload dicts and observations, not agents.
- Design section 6 says only that the budget study "runs on the CPU". It does not mention worker processes or sending agents between processes.
- The frozen wood checkpoint goes through `ResourceAgent.load(policy)` with the default `stage=WOOD_STAGE`, so it keeps the singleton. The wood stage under the default goal is unchanged on every real path.

Even when the defect fires, the damage is small. A copied wood file still reloads as wood, because load() compares `payload.get("stage", "wood")` with the stage name. Only the byte layout and digest differ. The stone refusal fails closed with a clear ValueError, not a silent wrong result. Low severity is right: a real robustness gap with no current trigger, and it fails safe.
verification.evidence:
Scratch script C:\Users\ethan\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-ethan-PycharmProjects-RL-Minecraft-project\e8caeeaf-7c0d-42d8-a0e0-47974dda527c\scratchpad\review\refute-stage-identity\check.py was run with PYTHONPATH set to the worktree and python -B. It loaded the frozen checkpoint results/pc_resource_runs/87673b8/mx-unmasked-q-train/policy.json:
- The loaded agent passes `stage is WOOD_STAGE` and saves keys ['format_version', 'environment', 'algorithm'], sha 8e81e881aae1. copy.copy gives the same.
- deepcopy and pickle clones have `is WOOD: False` and save keys ['format_version', 'stage', 'environment'], sha 61c621c82102. They still reload as wood.
- The stone agent from train_stone_simulator(5, seed=1) evaluates when original or copy.copy. deepcopy and pickle clones raise "A stone evaluation needs a stone-stage ResourceAgent".

Code: resources.py:236 has `@dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False)` and no custom reduce or copy hooks. Line 365 and stone.py:495 are quoted above. grep of minecraft_rl, infrastructure and scripts found no agent deepcopy, pickle or Pool. resource_server.py's only match is a comment about mkdir.

verification.fix_notes:
No change is needed before the overnight wood run: the defect cannot trigger from any current caller. The fix is cheap, so do it in S1 or before S5. Preferred fix: make StageSpec copies and pickles resolve to the registered singleton.
- Keep a module-level registry `_STAGES: dict[str, StageSpec]` in resources.py.
- Register WOOD_STAGE in it, and register STONE_STAGE when stone.py defines it.
- Add `def __reduce__(self): return (_registered_stage, (self.name,))` to StageSpec, where `_registered_stage(name)` imports minecraft_rl.stone lazily when name == 'stone' and returns `_STAGES[name]`. Both copy.deepcopy and pickle honour `__reduce__`, so the `is` checks keep working.

- In save, use `self.stage.name == WOOD_STAGE.name`. This is harmless: load() still validates actions, fields and caps against the loading stage.
- In evaluate_stone_policy, use `agent.stage.name != STONE_STAGE.name or tuple(agent.stage.actions) != STONE_STAGE.actions or agent.condition != STONE_CONDITION`.

- A deep-copied and an unpickled wood agent save bytes identical to the original agent's save. The test should compare against the original agent's save, not the on-disk checkpoint, which predates the initial_q key.

title: The stone reward pays +10 on the caller's success flag without checking that the observation shows a held stone pickaxe (and death is not checked against health)
failure_scenario: The design pays +10 only when the bridge confirms a held stone pickaxe. stone_reward_transition trusts its `success` and `death` arguments. In S3, if the coordinator passes a wrong flag (for example the wood-goal meaning of success, any wooden pickaxe, which is true on every stage-2 observation; or a stage-1 success flag carried over), every stone step would earn 9.99 even though the observation shows no stone pickaxe. Likewise death=True with health 20 gives -10.01, and health 0 with death=False is scored as an ordinary step. The simulator computes the flags correctly, so this matters only for the live coordinator.

The behaviour is real, and my scratch script reproduces it. stone_reward_transition takes the `success` and `death` flags as given: success=True with a wooden pickaxe held gives 9.99, death=True at health 20 gives -10.01, and health 0 with death=False gives -0.01. The stone function is deliberately "the wood reward's structure with Phi_stone".

(3) No S1 caller can pass a wrong flag. The only callers are the tests and StoneSimulator (stone.py ~388-395). The simulator computes success as stone_pickaxes > 0 and held_item == 'stone_pickaxe', and death as health == 0, which the reviewer concedes.

Seeds 120-149 are then used by only masking and initial-Q, which is not equal to the three names on the range, so the check fails with "name exactly these experiments on the range". Doing that breaks 100-119. The only fix is to split the range, which no message mentions. The builder's report says the opposite case fails (a range declared shared ahead of time); with two named experiments it passes (probe3 P7), so the strictness bites only with three or more.
evidence: probe3.py P5: "World seeds 120-149 are used by 2 experiments, but no range in configs/seed_registry.json declares them shared by exactly these: initial_q_experiment (...); resource_masking_experiment (...)". P7 (61000-61049 naming two experiments, both unused) printed no problems. Code: `if len(by) < 2 or (entries and set(entries[0]["experiments"]) == set(by)): continue`.
suggested_fix: Require set(by) to be a subset of the range's experiments, which together with coverage_problems already forces every user to be named. Or keep equality but have the message say to split the range at the seeds where the set of users changes.

verification.reasoning:
I reproduced the claim with my own probe. Line 326 of tests/test_seed_registry.py skips a seed only when `set(entries[0]["experiments"]) == set(by)`. This means every seed of a shared range has to be used by every experiment named on it. The rule is applied only when two or more experiments use a seed (`len(by) < 2` skips the rest). So the strictness only shows up once a range names three or more experiments and some of its seeds are used by only two of them.

The registry invites exactly that case. Range 100-149 says reuse is allowed for "training runs of a declared wood-stage experiment that states the reuse in its declaration and is added to this range", and a masked-budget rerun would use only 100-119.

What I saw, step by step:
- (A) A third experiment trains on 100-119 and is not yet named on the range. The coverage check says to name it on the range that holds those seeds.
- (B) After naming it on 100-149, the overlap check fails for 120-149, which only masking and initial-Q use. The message says to "name exactly these experiments on the range".
- Following that message literally means removing the third experiment from the range. That puts the registry back in state A, where coverage fails for 100-119. So the two messages contradict each other.
- (D) Splitting the range into 100-119 (three names) and 120-149 (two names) passes. The ranges stay non-overlapping, so the registry's form check accepts the split. No message mentions splitting.
- (E) If the third experiment uses all of 100-149, it passes.
- (F) A range naming two experiments that only one uses passes. This confirms the inconsistency: naming extra experiments on a range is allowed with one user but rejected with two.

The design does not ask for exact sets. Section 7.5 only says the test "fails on any overlap between experiments". The exact-set rule is the builder's own "strictest reading", stated in the build report.

Why the severity is low:
- The error only ever fails the test. It never lets an undeclared overlap or a held-out reuse through, because coverage_problems and held_out_problems catch those separately.
- The current tree passes: 20 tests, OK.
- Nothing in S1, the overnight wood run or the stone runs triggers it. It only matters for a future three-experiment reuse.
- A workaround exists (splitting the range); the messages just don't point to it.

- It matches the range's "is added to this range" reuse text.

- Update the asserted text at line 703 to match.

It should say to split the range at the seeds where the set of users changes (here into 100-119 and 120-149) and give each part exactly the experiments that use it. Even then, the "by" text on 100-149 should say that partial reuse needs a split.

None of this affects the wood stage, the frozen checkpoint or any S1 runtime code.

title: Declaration commands without --world-seed are ignored, although the registry's own seed rule says they play from 42
failure_scenario: A declaration lists "run.cmd resource-demo --random-baseline --condition unmasked --episodes 20" without --world-seed. The command would play worlds 42-61: 42-46 belong to wood development and 47-61 are unregistered. The test does not count it at all, which contradicts the registry's seed_rule ("--world-seed defaults to 42"). The skip was added so that the benchmark's 'arm' prose would not be counted.
evidence: probe2.py P3d: a declaration whose commands field holds that command produced no problem. Code: `if "--world-seed" not in segment: continue` (line 137), and the docstring "A command without --world-seed describes a run whose seeds a plan sets, so it is not counted."
suggested_fix: Count a command without --world-seed as 42 to 42 + episodes - 1 when it starts with run.cmd or python -m infrastructure. Treat a bare mention such as the benchmark's 'arm' text as prose, or exempt it by an explicit marker.

verification.reasoning:
The behaviour the reviewer describes is real. I reproduced it: a declaration whose commands field holds "run.cmd resource-demo --random-baseline --condition unmasked --episodes 20" produces no uses and no problems. The same command with "--world-seed 42" adds range(42, 62). It is still not a defect against the spec, for four reasons.

(1) The design does not ask for this. Section 7.5 of docs/stone_tools_design.md (line 583) requires the test to expand "every configs/*.json plan and every retained metadata.json (first_world_seed plus episodes_requested)" and fail on overlaps between experiments. Reading declaration prose and listed commands at all goes beyond that. Plans and metadata are fully covered.

(2) The skip is deliberate and documented. The docstring of command_seeds says so, and the builder's report (build_reports.txt line 242) gives the reason: the benchmark's "arm" text names resource-demo without seeds because the plans set them.

(3) The real use is caught where the design puts the check. A run started without --world-seed writes first_world_seed=42 into its metadata.json (infrastructure/resource_session.py:281). Once that run is retained, survey() counts it, for example results/resource_smoke/resource-smoke-online at 42. For a stone experiment, coverage_problems would then flag both 42-46 (a wood_resource_development range, not one of its own) and 47-61 (unregistered). The registry's seed_rule describes how a run maps to seeds, which is what the metadata path applies. It does not promise that commands in a declaration are parsed.

(4) No current or planned config has such a command. Every run.cmd resource-train/demo line in configs/resource_masking_experiment.json names --world-seed. The initial-Q declaration's command is resource-parallel with a plan. The test suite passes (20 tests OK).

What remains is an optional early warning for a typo in a future declaration that has not been run. It cannot change the wood stage, the bot's safety, or any seed already used.

title: Prose checks block teammates on non-world seeds and placeholder commands
failure_scenario: In any config, the text "three learner seeds 0 to 2", "random seeds 0-3" or "simulator study over seeds 0-19" fails, because NOT_WORLDS only knows agent, simulator and episode as the word just before. A continuation described as "resource-train --policy <saved> --world-seed <next seed> --episodes <remaining>" also fails as a non-integer command. The check is also weak in the other direction: "seeds 1-3" passes only because 1-3 happens to be a development range.
evidence: probe2.py P3e: "configs/stone_pickaxe_experiment.json mentions world seeds 0, which no range ... covers" and "... mentions world seeds 0, 4-19 ...". P3f: "continuation: a command's --world-seed or --episodes is not an integer: 'resource-train --policy <saved policy.json> --world-seed <next seed> --episodes <remaining>'".
suggested_fix: Widen NOT_WORLDS (learner, random, python, study, simulator-study) or look at the two words before the match. Ignore commands whose --world-seed value is a <placeholder>. Keep the advice to reword.

verification.reasoning:
The behaviour the reviewer describes is real, but it is not a defect.

1. The mention check is a deliberate fail-closed lint. A hit only means "no range covers this", and the message tells the author what to do: "register them, or reword the text if they are not world seeds". Fixing a false positive is one word (for example "agent seeds 0 to 2"), so nobody is blocked for good.

2. The design does not ask for prose checking at all. docs/stone_tools_design.md section 7.5 only asks that the test expand every configs/*.json plan and every retained metadata.json and fail on any overlap between experiments. The prose check is an extra the builder added on top. Nothing in the design requires it to accept free-form non-world-seed prose.

3. No current or planned text trips it. The suite passes at c441c5f (20 tests OK). The design's own wording for the stone learners passes: "agent seeds 0, 1 and 2" (section 8) does not match the range pattern, and "agent seeds 0 to 2" is skipped. The stone declaration is committed at S7, after the S5 study fixes N, so it has no reason to list `--episodes <N>` or `--world-seed <next seed>` templates. The existing declarations describe continuations in plain prose and pass.

4. The "weak in the other direction" point is intended behaviour. mention_problems checks registration by any range, not ownership, because declarations legitimately mention other experiments' seeds. For example, initial_q_experiment.json says "Seeds 20000-20019 are not reused". Requiring ownership there would be wrong. The real ownership, overlap and held-out checks run on plans, world_seeds fields, numeric commands and metadata, not on prose.

5. Refusing a command whose --world-seed is not an integer is also fail-closed on purpose. If the test cannot tell which worlds a declared command plays, it says so rather than skipping the command. The reviewer's fix (ignore placeholder seeds) would let a declared command's worlds go unchecked.

6. Widening NOT_WORLDS with more words (learner, random, python, study, ...) is open-ended whack-a-mole and adds nothing the reword advice does not already give.

Severity: low at most, and only as an ergonomic note. It has no bearing on the wood stage or on any stone safety helper.

title: Only top-level configs/*.json files are surveyed
failure_scenario: A plan committed as configs/stone/stone_survey_plan.json, or anywhere outside configs/ (resource-parallel accepts any plan path), is never read. Its seeds go unchecked until its runs are retained.
evidence: `for file in sorted((root / "configs").glob("*.json")):`, and parallel_runs.resource_parallel takes any path ("Plan JSON file, normally committed under configs/").
suggested_fix: Use rglob("*.json") under configs/, or fail on any .json file in a subfolder of configs/.

verification.reasoning:
The code does what the reviewer says. survey() (tests/test_seed_registry.py:222) and test_the_plan_expansion_matches_the_scheduler (line 601) both use the non-recursive `(root / "configs").glob("*.json")`, so a plan anywhere else in the repo is never read. The scheduler does not stop this either: code_state() (infrastructure/parallel_runs.py:399-408) only requires the plan to be committed somewhere under the repo root, and the CLI help says only "normally committed under configs/".

I reproduced it offline. In a temp copy of configs/, I added a plan whose train job uses world seeds 20000-20004 (part of the held-out test range of resource_masking_experiment):
- At configs/zz_new_plan.json it fails with 4 problems (unregistered, cross-experiment overlap, held-out reuse).
- At configs/stone/zz_new_plan.json it gives 0 problems and is never surveyed.
- The same subfolder file, also added to initial_q_experiment's "sources" in the registry, still gives 0 problems. registry_problems() only checks that the source exists, so the file passes as registered while its seeds are never expanded.
- At plans/zz_new_plan.json (outside configs/) it gives 0 problems.

This is more than the reviewer stated. The registry's own instruction says "add it to its experiment's sources and register its seeds", so following it for a subfolder file gives a false pass. That is a hole in the module's stated guarantee ("Every world seed a plan, a declaration or a retained run uses is registered").

Why the severity stays low:
- The design (section 7.5) literally specifies "expands every `configs/*.json` plan", and the code matches that wording.
- Every current config and every planned one (configs/stone_pickaxe_experiment.json, configs/stone_pickaxe_plan.json) is top-level. configs/ has no subfolders today, so nothing is missed now.
- Retained metadata.json is still checked afterwards, though only after the worlds have been played.
- It has no effect on the wood stage, the default goal or the stone safety helpers.

So this is a robustness gap against future placement, not a current failure. It is not refuted, because the test plainly and silently skips a registered source.

title: Most S2 survey staircase data will be the table-adjacency refusal, not the terrain
failure_scenario: S2 runs the survey at the hand-off cell, which is CRAFT_PICKAXE's position next to the own table. surveyStaircases plans all four headings from that cell with ctx.table = ownTable. planStairStep (stone-helpers.js:449) refuses any column within Chebyshev 1 of the table as near_own_table, and it does so before any liquid, gravity, cave, floor or dig-time check. So for most headings the survey never tests the terrain, and for a bot standing on its table it records no staircase at all. The design does not simulate its own pre-step moves either (stepped_off_table, centring, moved_along_surface, section 4.4). S2 exists to measure 'how often each check refuses' before the depth cap and budgets are frozen (design 7.6), but its per-heading refusal counts will mostly show the table rule, so the terrain refusal rates are not measured.
evidence: review/plumbing/handoff_table.py looked at the 302 successful retained 87673b8 episodes that have a table. Bot-to-table Chebyshev distance: {0: 6, 1: 249, 2: 36, 3: 9, 4: 2}. Headings refused near_own_table at step 1: {0: 16, 1: 31, 2: 17, 3: 232, 4: 6}. That is 785 of 1208 heading starts (65%) refused before any terrain check, and 6 hand-offs (bot on the table) give no staircase data at all. review/plumbing/survey_table.js on the worked example: no table gives '+x:stone_exposed(1/2/3/3/2) +z:stone_exposed(...) -x:stone_exposed(...) -z:stone_exposed(...)'; table orthogonally adjacent gives '+x:near_own_table() +z:near_own_table() -x:stone_exposed(1/2/3/3/2) -z:near_own_table()'; table diagonal gives two near_own_table. The J2 builder report predicted this ('Expect frequent near_own_table refusals in the survey'), and it was not addressed.
suggested_fix: In stoneSurveyRecord, add a second per-heading simulation with the near_own_table rule turned off, for example a flag in ctx that planStairStep honours. Keep digVerdict's own_table refusal, so a plan never digs through the table. Record it as e.g. staircases_ignoring_table. Also record the bot's column offset from the table, and for an on-table hand-off simulate from the natural cell that DIG_DOWN's step-off would use. S2 can then separate the table rule from the terrain.

verification.reasoning:
I checked the code and the reviewer is right. stoneSurveyRecord (resource-bridge.js:573-591) calls surveyStaircases(world, feet, {...scan.ctx, startY, reversible}) (resource-bridge.js:560-567). scan.ctx carries table: ownTable (resource-bridge.js:890). planStaircase runs planStairStep for each heading and stops at the first refusal. planStairStep (stone-helpers.js:449) returns near_own_table for any column within Chebyshev distance 1 of the table column. It does this right after the margin check and before it reads any cell, so it comes before the liquid, gravity, dig-time, cave_below, landing and reversibility checks. A heading that starts next to the table therefore ends at step 1 and records no terrain data.

The design backs the reviewer. Section 7.6 says the survey records "what planStairStep would refuse on each heading for 6 steps". Section 4.4 lists planStairStep's per-step checks as digVerdict, floor, landing, dig time, margin, depth and reversibility. Dropping headings near the table is a separate rule under "Choosing the heading": "Among the headings whose first step passes: 1. drop headings within one column of the bot's own table". The builder moved that rule inside planStairStep and applied it on every step. Their report calls this "the stricter reading" (build_reports.txt:22). It is safe, but it changes what the survey measures compared with the spec. The builder also predicted the effect ("Expect frequent near_own_table refusals in the survey", :347) and left it as an open question (:354).

Why I lowered the severity from medium to low:
- It is diagnostic only. It is not a safety problem, because the rule is stricter, never looser.
- The wood stage is untouched. The survey runs only with --stone-survey, inside the try/catch that records errors under the wood goal.
- depth_to_stone is computed in the bot's own column and is unaffected, and it is the main input for the depth cap.
- The headings that are still tested (about 1.4 per hand-off) are exactly the ones the live DIG_DOWN could use from that cell.
- Seeds 61000-61049 are declared reusable, so S2 (about 30 minutes) can be rerun cheaply.

The cost is real, though. If S2 runs before a fix, about 65% of heading starts carry no terrain refusal data and the 6 on-table hand-offs carry none at all. The terrain refusal and budget statistics would then rest on roughly a third of the intended sample.
